notes: Sprinkler timer guide series (owner GO 2026-09-05; scope in docs/irrigation-controller-guide-scope.md). Hub-only informational posts that teach a lawn customer to run the irrigation controller on their own wall, one brand per post. GLOBAL RULES, all briefs: (1) informational lane only — no near-me or transactional phrasing anywhere; (2) MANUAL-FIRST: the primary how-to is running the controller BY HAND, following the customer's weekly Waves watering plan for that week. THE PLAN DOES NOT ALWAYS CARRY PER-ZONE MINUTES: where the head type is missing or mixed it gives an events-only "full cycle" instruction instead, so every routine needs a branch that follows the plan's own full-cycle wording rather than telling the reader to enter minutes that were never supplied. THE PLAN IS AUTHORITATIVE FOR CADENCE AND THE GUIDE NEVER HARDCODES ONE: the plan decides how many runs that week (it can be more than one on a two-day permission), and whether to skip entirely (the plan does NOT choose or name the weekday — it says only "your permitted watering day", so the assigned day or days come from the county or address lookup), and whether to skip an INDIVIDUAL run for rain. THE RAIN CHECK IS NOT A SPECIAL CASE: the weekly email attaches it to EVERY run plan, flagged or not, so the guide must tell the reader to check before every run — hand or scheduled — and skip just that run when half an inch or more has fallen (measured since the previous permitted watering day, except the first run of the week, which is measured from the start of the week). So write "follow this week's plan" and "each run it asks for", never "once a week", and cover all FOUR cases the plan can present: run; check the rain before each run and skip just that one; a hold week, which is usually CONDITIONAL — the plan itself says to run a fallback cycle if the grass shows wilt cues, or if the reader did not run the previous week — so never flatten a hold into "do nothing"; and a week where watering is not permitted at all, which is the only unconditional no-watering case. Whatever the plan says that week is what the reader does: quote its condition, never replace it — OFF is the resting position between runs ONLY where every zone is manual — OFF disables all zones, so in a mixed yard whose beds or drip still run automatically the controller stays in its normal run position and the grass zones are separated out instead; wherever OFF is recommended, this qualification must appear with it; a programmed schedule is the optional section at the END of the post; (3) every controller mechanic (dial positions, button names, manual-run steps, rain delay, sensor bypass) must match the cited manufacturer manual — if the manual does not support a step, OMIT it; never invent a button. Where a manufacturer blocks automated requests and no manual can be fetched (Hunter), the owner-reviewed Waves brand guide named in that brief's sources is the authority instead, and no control it does not describe may be introduced; (4) the weekly plan NEVER names weekday(s) — it carries the number of runs and the minutes, and speaks only of 'your permitted watering day' — so a schedule section must send the reader to their county or address lookup for the assigned weekday(s) and use the plan only for how many runs and how long; NEVER state a number of allowed watering days per week, an assigned weekday, or allowed hours — watering-day rules come from the customer's county and the current water-shortage order and change; say 'your assigned day and your county's allowed hours' and point to the county; (5) a hand run counts the same as a scheduled one for those rules — say so; (6) Waves does NOT repair irrigation: if a zone will not run, a head is broken, or the box faults, the reader is referred to an irrigation contractor — never imply Waves services, installs, or repairs sprinklers; (7) never describe any product or application as 'safe'; never state prices or dollar amounts — for controller pricing say 'check current pricing'; (8) no manufacturer imagery or scraped photos: hero and body images are generated or Waves-owned, and no manual text is reproduced — link the official manual instead; (9) the weekly Waves watering plan may be mentioned only as 'the weekly watering plan Waves lawn customers receive' — never promise it names the day, never state how many runs it will ask for, and never imply it always asks for the same number; (10) internal links: the lawn treatment prep page and the overwatering-vs-underwatering post at minimum. (11) every post links one lawn care city service page (/lawn-care-{city}-fl/) in the body — the quality gate's hub-link hard check requires it.

briefs.thesis: Rain Bird's dial controllers (ESP-TM2, ESP-Me/Me3) are among the timers we most often find on Southwest Florida homes and straightforward to run by hand once you know the dial — which is all most homeowners need (make no cross-brand ranking; no source here compares brands): a hand run for each run this week's plan asks for, with that week's minutes (the plan may ask for more than one, for none, or for a rain check before each), the dial back on OFF between runs where every zone is manual, and the programmed schedule left for the few who want it. Frame prevalence explicitly as our own field experience; state no market share, ranking or figure, and attribute it to no source.
outline: Quick answer: which Rain Bird you have (where the model name is printed), and the weekly move in one line — read this week's plan (see the plan section), then run the grass zones by hand for each run it asks for, and rest the dial on OFF between runs where every zone is manual (keep the normal run position if beds or drip have their own schedules). Do not restate the plan rules here — point the reader to the plan section for how many runs, how many minutes, hold weeks and the rain check.

What this week's plan is telling you — the single place the post explains WHEN and HOW MUCH, referenced by every other section rather than repeated: (a) HOW MANY runs it asks for, which can be more than one; (b) the minutes per grass zone — or, when your saved head type is missing or mixed, no minutes at all and a full cycle by events instead, in which case follow the plan's own full-cycle wording and never invent a number; (c) a hold week, which usually carries a CONDITION rather than meaning nothing (run a fallback cycle if the grass shows wilt cues, or if you did not run the previous week) — only a week when watering is not permitted at all means no run; (d) the rain check, which applies before EVERY run whether it is by hand or scheduled: if half an inch or more has fallen before that run (measured since your previous permitted watering day when the plan asks for more than one — except the FIRST run of the week, which is measured from the start of this week, so rain that fell after last week's final watering day but before this week began does not cancel it), skip THAT run, not the week; (e) the plan never names a weekday — it says 'your permitted watering day', so the assigned day or days come from your county's watering-restriction lookup. A hand run counts exactly the same as a scheduled one under those rules.

A short history of Rain Bird: founded 1933 in Glendora, California, around Orton Englehart's horizontal-action impact sprinkler; still family-owned; headquartered in Azusa — verified against rainbird.com/about, dates omitted if the page does not state them

The models you will actually find on a Southwest Florida wall: ESP-TM2 (the builder-grade dial box we routinely find on newer homes — field experience only, no "most" and no market-share claim), ESP-Me and ESP-Me3 (expandable, up to 22 zones, LNK2 Wi-Fi option on the Me3), ESP-RZXe (button faceplate, no dial), SST (simple push-button unit) — one paragraph each, what the faceplate looks like, who it suits

Honest review — pros (as our own hands-on opinion, explicitly labelled as such, never as a sourced ranking): the dial programming is straightforward; manual watering is one dial position; Seasonal Adjust is one knob; parts and manuals are everywhere; cons: multiple start-time slots per program hide an inherited builder schedule, and how many slots and programs a model has differs between them — take the count from that model's own manual rather than quoting one number for the range; the OFF position is the only sure resting state; the Wi-Fi module costs extra; the SST has no per-zone flexibility beyond its buttons. Include a ComparisonTable of the four models (dial or buttons, max zones, manual-run control, Wi-Fi option, best for) with NO prices, and an HonestRejection: who should not bother upgrading or programming a schedule at all

How to run it by hand, per model — CONTROLS ONLY (HowTo, visible numbered steps); when and how much comes from the plan section: ESP-TM2 — MANUAL STATION is a ONE-ZONE operation, so describe it as such; for the whole lawn use the stored-program manual start the linked manual gives (dial to AUTO RUN, select the program, hold the start control until it begins), exactly as the published Waves Rain Bird guide describes it. ESP-Me3 — dial to Manual Watering, set minutes, press Hold to Start until STARTED, turn the dial to AUTO. ESP-Me, RZXe and SST — no manual for these is cited in this brief, so give NO button sequence: describe the faceplate and send the reader to the Rain Bird support center for that model. MIXED YARDS: a whole-program start runs EVERY station in that program, so start a program by hand only when it is verified to hold grass zones alone (or is an unused program you set up for the lawn); otherwise run the grass zones one at a time with the one-station control and leave the shared program untouched. Update the stored RUN TIMES from the current plan before any stored-program start — stored numbers go stale. After a run, return the dial to OFF the same day ONLY when every zone is manual; if beds or drip run on their own schedules, leave the dial in its normal run position or OFF disables their watering indefinitely.

Why OFF is the resting position, and the one-time check: with the dial on OFF nothing waters (Rain Bird's own manual says so); before the first hand run, on the ESP-TM2 and ESP-Me3 ONLY (the models whose manuals are cited here — for the ESP-Me, RZXe and SST describe the purpose of this check and send the reader to the Rain Bird support center for their model's own steps), step through EVERY start-time slot in EVERY program the model has — the count differs by model, so take it from that model's manual rather than assuming three programs and four slots — and set to OFF only the slots belonging to grass-only programs, so a builder's leftover lawn schedule cannot fire while the dial sits in a run position. In a mixed yard, LEAVE the start times that drive bed or drip programs alone and remove the grass zones from those programs instead; clearing their starts is the same mistake as leaving the dial on OFF

Watering rules: a hand run counts the same as a scheduled one — run it only on your assigned day and inside your county's allowed hours; those come from the county and the current water-shortage order and change, so check the county page; Waves lawn customers get a weekly watering plan with the minutes per zone and what to do that week — which may be one run or more than one, a rain check before each run, or a hold that usually still carries a condition

Want it to run itself? The optional schedule (dial models): DATE/TIME with AM/PM checked twice; ONE program verified to hold grass zones only — use an unused program if program A already drives beds or drip, and never repoint an existing non-turf program; one start time chosen so the WHOLE cycle (the sum of every enabled zone's run time) both begins and finishes inside the allowed hours, with the other slots OFF; RUN TIMES per zone; RUN DAYS = the assigned day or days for your address from your county's watering-restriction lookup, covering every day the plan's run count needs; dial back to AUTO RUN. Rain delay (ONLY where every automatic program may pause together — a controller-wide delay also stops bed and drip programs, so in a mixed yard suppress the grass program alone) = dial on AUTO RUN, hold the + button, set days remaining. Leave SEASONAL ADJUST at 100%, because a percentage set once scales every later run-time entry. Rain-sensor handling differs between these models — give the control path each model's own linked manual describes, under that model's heading, and note that a hand-started run may ignore the sensor where the manual says so. Maintaining it: a schedule repeats a fixed cadence and fixed minutes, so each week update the stored run times when the plan's minutes change AND the scheduled run days when the plan's run count changes, and suppress any run the plan does not want. Suppression must be event-scoped: one start time is shared by every selected run day, so clearing it to skip ONE run also cancels the later ones the plan may still want — use a per-event pause where the model offers one, otherwise write the original start down and restore it BEFORE the next assigned day, since a cleared start stays cleared. Do not restate the plan rules here — point the reader to the plan section for how many runs, how many minutes, hold weeks and the rain check.

When the sprinklers will not run: Waves does not repair irrigation — a zone that will not come on, a broken head, or a box fault goes to an irrigation contractor; Waves still tells you what to water and when

OFF is the resting position ONLY where every zone is manual. Every instruction to return the dial to OFF must carry the mixed-yard caveat — OFF disables bed and drip schedules indefinitely, which is the fastest way for this post to cost a reader their landscaping. Keep AUTO RUN in mixed yards and remove the grass zones or start times from the automatic programs instead.

Every ordered weekly sequence is gated on the plan for that week, and the plan's wording for that week is what the reader follows — including the condition a hold week usually carries. Never state a blanket rule that a skip means no run; the only unconditional no-watering case is a week where irrigation is not permitted at all.

The optional schedule is maintained weekly, exactly like the manual routine: refresh the stored run times when the plan changes the minutes, refresh the scheduled RUN DAYS / Water Days when the plan changes how many runs it asks for, and suppress a run the plan does not want. Never present a programmed schedule as set-and-forget.

Prescribe exact controls ONLY for models whose manual is cited in sources — ESP-TM2 and ESP-Me3, and no others. For the ESP-Me, the RZXe and the SST, describe the faceplate and point to the Rain Bird support center — do not name buttons or give a sequence for a model whose manual is not linked here.

Cadence comes from the weekly plan, never from this post: it may call for one run or more than one, for skipping the week, or for checking the rain before each individual run and skipping only that one. Write every routine as "do what this week's plan says, for each run it asks for". Never say "once a week" and never treat skip as an all-or-nothing week.

Any controller-wide pause (rain delay, SYSTEM OFF, OFF) stops EVERY zone. Wherever one is offered, say so and give mixed-yard readers a grass-program-only alternative — this is the same failure mode as the OFF advice, in a different control.

Stored minutes go stale: the weekly plan recalculates minutes from current demand and carryover, so every stored-program run must be preceded by updating RUN TIMES for the grass zones from that week's plan. Never write "store the minutes once".

A hold ("skip") week is usually CONDITIONAL: the plan tells the reader to run a fallback cycle if the grass shows wilt cues, or if they did not run the previous week. Never write "skip means do nothing" as a blanket rule — say to follow the plan's own wording for that week, and reserve unconditional no-watering for a week where irrigation is not permitted at all.

The weekly plan does not name weekdays and cannot: it says "your permitted watering day". Anywhere the reader must choose RUN DAYS / Water Days, send them to their county or address lookup for the assigned day(s), and use the plan only for how many runs and how many minutes.

No cross-brand ranking. The sources here are single-brand manuals and a single-brand guide; nothing compares usability across manufacturers. Any preference must read explicitly as our own hands-on opinion, never as an established fact or a superlative.

The weekly plan does not always include per-zone minutes: where the head type is missing or mixed it prescribes a full cycle by events instead. Never write a step that assumes a minutes figure exists - give the events-only path in the plan's own wording alongside the minutes path, and never invent a number when none is supplied.

A half-inch of rain skips ONE run, on every plan - not just the weeks the plan flags as rain-conditional. Every routine in the post, manual and scheduled, must carry the check before each run and suppress only that run.

One-time setup: FIRST confirm PROGRAM A holds grass zones only — the one-touch right-arrow start always runs program A, which is why the grass minutes must live there and not in B or C, and why an unused program is NOT an option for this hand-run path. Where beds or drip share program A, skip this setup entirely and run the grass zones with Manual One Station; then store the plan's minutes in grass-only program A under Run Times, clear every start-time slot the model provides in grass-only programs (leaving untouched any start that drives a bed or drip program, and removing the grass zones from those programs instead), and rest the dial on SYSTEM OFF only if every zone is manual. Each run: update Run Times for every grass zone from the current plan (stored numbers go stale), dial to RUN, hold the right arrow about two seconds for the one-touch start, LET THE WHOLE CYCLE FINISH (add up the zone minutes so the reader knows how long that is — moving the dial off RUN stops the run), and only then return the dial to SYSTEM OFF, the same day, where every zone is manual. MIXED YARDS: keep the bed and drip programs, zero the grass zones inside them, leave the dial on RUN, and use Manual One Station for grass.

Hydrawise owners: run grass zones from the app or touchscreen for the plan’s minutes, schedule beds and drip SEPARATELY according to their own irrigation guidance — do not tell readers those zones need shorter runs than turf; emitter output and plant demand set those durations, and the weekly plan’s minutes are turf-only — and remove grass zones from automatic programs rather than deleting programs other zones still need

Every ordered weekly sequence is gated on the plan for that week, and the plan's wording for that week is what the reader follows — including the condition a hold week usually carries. Never state a blanket rule that a skip means no run; the only unconditional no-watering case is a week where irrigation is not permitted at all.

The optional schedule is maintained weekly, exactly like the manual routine: refresh the stored run times when the plan changes the minutes, refresh the scheduled RUN DAYS / Water Days when the plan changes how many runs it asks for, and suppress a run the plan does not want. Never present a programmed schedule as set-and-forget.

Cadence comes from the weekly plan, never from this post: it may call for one run or more than one, for skipping the week, or for checking the rain before each individual run and skipping only that one. Write every routine as "do what this week's plan says, for each run it asks for". Never say "once a week" and never treat skip as an all-or-nothing week.

Any controller-wide pause (rain delay, SYSTEM OFF, OFF) stops EVERY zone. Wherever one is offered, say so and give mixed-yard readers a grass-program-only alternative — this is the same failure mode as the OFF advice, in a different control.

Any SCHEDULED-OPERATION procedure that moves the dial off RUN must end by putting it back on RUN — setting a rain delay from SYSTEM OFF is the case that matters — or the controller is left disabled and the schedule never fires. This does NOT apply to the manual-first weekly run, which deliberately ends on SYSTEM OFF where every zone is manual. Check that each sequence ends in the position its own mode needs, rather than forcing one ending on all of them.

A hold ("skip") week is usually CONDITIONAL: the plan tells the reader to run a fallback cycle if the grass shows wilt cues, or if they did not run the previous week. Never write "skip means do nothing" as a blanket rule — say to follow the plan's own wording for that week, and reserve unconditional no-watering for a week where irrigation is not permitted at all.

The weekly plan does not name weekdays and cannot: it says "your permitted watering day". Anywhere the reader must choose RUN DAYS / Water Days, send them to their county or address lookup for the assigned day(s), and use the plan only for how many runs and how many minutes.

No cross-brand ranking. The sources here are single-brand manuals and a single-brand guide; nothing compares usability across manufacturers. Any preference must read explicitly as our own hands-on opinion, never as an established fact or a superlative.

The weekly plan does not always include per-zone minutes: where the head type is missing or mixed it prescribes a full cycle by events instead. Never write a step that assumes a minutes figure exists - give the events-only path in the plan's own wording alongside the minutes path, and never invent a number when none is supplied.

A half-inch of rain skips ONE run, on every plan - not just the weeks the plan flags as rain-conditional. Every routine in the post, manual and scheduled, must carry the check before each run and suppress only that run.
